performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: The Sanctus is the third movement of Fauré’s Requiem, Op. 48. The sopranos sing a three-note “Sanctus” over harp and divided violas, the brass play only in a single “Hosanna”, and the movement ends as quietly as it began.

sections.label: A · Sanctus exchanged between sopranos and men
A′ · Vocal phrases at higher pitch
sections.mNote: Wider vocal phrases over continuing harp and viola figures

sections.label: A″ · Harp arpeggios return
sections.mNote: The choir returns to “Sanctus” above quiet strings.

cues.title: Opening of the Sanctus
cues.text: The harp plays rising E♭ major arpeggios while two viola parts move around each other. The sopranos sing “Sanctus” on three notes, and the men reply. The organ holds the harmony.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 45–47: harp, divided violas, sustained organ and the choral exchanges. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1900
cues.text: Paul Taffanel conducted the expanded Requiem at the Trocadéro in Paris on 12 July 1900, with the Société des concerts du Conservatoire. Before the score was printed, Fauré’s publisher, Julien Hamelle, had advised him to prepare a version for full symphony orchestra.
cues.evidence: First performance on 12 July 1900 at the Trocadéro, Société des concerts du Conservatoire, Paul Taffanel conducting: IMSLP work page, https://imslp.org/wiki/Requiem,_Op.48_(Faur%C3%A9,_Gabriel) ; date and venue also in Wadham Sutton’s Hyperion note, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4018_68209 . Hamelle’s advice to prepare a version for large symphony orchestra before publishing: Jean-Michel Nectoux, booklet note for Harmonia Mundi HMM 931292, https://www.harmoniamundi.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/931292_booklet.pdf . The claim of 250 performers, which rested on Wikipedia’s citation of Nectoux (1991), is not used.

cues.title: Violin section, 1900 version
cues.text: The church orchestra of 1893 had no violin section. The concert version of 1900 added one. In the Sanctus the first and second violins, muted, play a flowing line above the harp’s arpeggios.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), p. 45: “1ers et 2ds Violons”, marked “Sourdines”; p. 51: the violin line above the harp. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf . The 1893 orchestration “pas de violons, pas de bois” (with a solo violin credited in the Sanctus): Nectoux, Harmonia Mundi HMM 931292 booklet, https://www.harmoniamundi.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/931292_booklet.pdf . A full body of violins in the 1900 version’s Sanctus: Wadham Sutton, Hyperion note, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4018_68209 . Fauré’s remark to Ysaÿe on the “angelic” violins (Nectoux 1991, as cited on Wikipedia) could not be traced to an opened source and is not used.

cues.title: Hosanna, brass fanfare
cues.text: The sopranos begin the “Hosanna” softly. As the phrase grows, the harp changes from running notes to chords, and horns and trumpets play a fanfare. Above them the men’s voices sing “Hosanna in excelsis”.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 54–57: soprano Hosanna, chordal harp and strings, and the brass fanfare beneath the men’s voices.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the harp arpeggios
cues.text: After the brass fanfare comes a diminuendo. The harp arpeggios return, the violas resume their running figures and the choir sings “Sanctus” again, pianissimo. The altos, who have not sung until now, join for the closing prayer.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 57–60: diminuendo, returning harp and viola figures, and the altos’ first entry.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Longer choral phrases at “Dominus Deus Sabaoth”
transitions.from: A · Sanctus exchanged between sopranos and men
transitions.to: A′ · Vocal phrases at higher pitch
transitions.how: The harp and divided violas continue their flowing figures. Above them, at “Dominus Deus Sabaoth”, the sopranos move beyond the short three-note phrase of “Sanctus”. The men answer the longer line, and the organ sustains beneath both groups.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 49–51: the wider choral phrases over continuing harp and viola figures.

transitions.title: Sopranos over divided violins
transitions.from: A′ · Vocal phrases at higher pitch
transitions.how: The men rest while the sopranos sing “Pleni sunt coeli et terra”, marked sempre dolce. Divided violins play their line above the harp, and the cellos hold sustained notes arco. The men return at “gloria tua”.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 52–53, rehearsal C: soprano phrase, divided violins and arco cellos.

transitions.title: Running notes become a fanfare
transitions.how: From rehearsal D the sopranos begin “Hosanna” softly over the continuing viola figures. The harp and strings then change to repeated chords, and the bass beat grows firmer. Horns and trumpets enter forte, and the men sing their “Hosanna” above this fanfare.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 54–57: the build from rehearsal D to the brass-supported Hosanna.

transitions.title: Brass diminuendo and return to E♭
transitions.how: The sopranos’ answering phrase diminishes, and the brass drop to pianissimo. The harp resumes its broken E♭ major chords, and the lower strings change from pizzicato to arco. Over the organ’s sustained harmony the choir sings “Sanctus” once more.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 57–60: brass diminuendo, harp arpeggios, arco strings and closing Sanctus.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: III. Sanctus, printed pp. 45–60: harp and divided violas, choral answers, violins, the double-bass entry on p. 51 and brass fanfares. The violins rest during the loud Hosanna on pp. 55–58.

timeline.note: The harp plays rising figures while two viola lines move against one another. The organ holds an E♭ major chord.
The sopranos sing three notes on “Sanctus”. The men answer, with cellos underneath.
Pianissimo violins enter above the moving harp and violas.
The sopranos sing “Pleni sunt coeli” and the men answer. Violins climb above the harp; cellos and double basses support them.
Horns and trumpets sound a forte fanfare. The men sing “Hosanna” over emphatic lower-string chords; the violins rest.
The brass drop to pianissimo. The harp arpeggios return, and the low strings play arco again.
The brass stop. A violin melody rises over harp arpeggios and sustained low strings.
The altos join the final “Sanctus”. Harp and strings continue around the quiet choral chords.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.51 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 3 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+60 cents (CQT histogram) and −0.38 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning); the report’s pitch-class labels read E♭ major as E major, which places the offset on the sharp side); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: Organist and teacher who wrote songs and chamber music in an unusual harmonic language.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
As a boy, Fauré often went into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and Gabriel Fauré’s first musical experiences were on the small instrument in its chapel. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he studied plainchant, the organ and the polyphony of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was over, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers well outside their syllabus. Saint-Saëns became Fauré’s teacher, champion and friend, and remained so for sixty years. Fauré left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine, a setting of a French prayer over a flowing keyboard part, in which each new choral entry joins a phrase already under way.
